ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The results were discussed with the steering committee, Van Rens Foundation and the Medical Research Ethics Committee and it was decided to continue the trial.
After providing written informed consent, patients were randomized 1:1 to the dual mobility cup group or the unipolar cup group using the Castor electronic data capture system (7).
table.formatted: After providing written informed consent, patients were randomized 1:1 to the dual mobility cup group or the unipolar cup group using the Castor electronic data capture system <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(7)</ref>.

table.text: In this population, patients are analyzed in the group they were randomized to, regardless of the type of cup they received and the surgical approach used.
I.e. patients who were randomized to a DM cup but instead received a UP cup will then be assigned to the UP cup group, and vice versa.

To participate in the study, a patient must meet all the following criteria: • Patients eligible for elective primary THA with a 32mm or 36mm liner, for any indication • THA using a posterolateral surgical approach • Patients ≥ 70 years old • Adequate comprehension of written and spoken Dutch or Spanish (for patients in the Vall d'Hebron University Hospital) Patients meeting any of the following criteria are excluded from participation in the study: Exclusion criteria • Patients unable to complete PROMs • Patients with dementia, epilepsy, spasticity, mental retardation, or alcoholism (If dementia or mental retardation is not already mentioned in the medical chart, this can be determined by doctors' opinion) • Patients not eligible for either a unipolar or dual mobility cup

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: The sample size was calculated for the primary outcome and was based on anticipated 1-year dislocation risks of 4% in the unipolar cup group and 1% in the dual mobility cup group. To show the superiority of dual mobility cups compared to unipolar cups with respect to the number of patients who suffer a hip dislocation within 1 year after primary THA, with at least 80% power at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, 976 patients (488 in each group) would need to participate. To account for loss to follow-up, 550 patients are recruited per arm (1,100 total randomized).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: effect_size, effect_size_metric, software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "unknown", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 1100, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.8, effect_size = NA_real_, effect_size_metric = NA_character_, software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "The sample size was calculated for the primary outcome and was based on anticipated 1-year dislocation risks of 4% in the unipolar cup group and 1% in the dual mobility cup group. To show the superiority of dual mobility cups compared to unipolar cups with respect to the number of patients who suffer a hip dislocation within 1 year after primary THA, with at least 80% power at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, 976 patients (488 in each group) would need to participate. To account for loss to follow-up, 550 patients are recruited per arm (1,100 total randomized)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 2 detected *p* values.

table.expanded: Decision: At the interim analysis, 0 dislocations occurred in 101 patients (0%) in the dual mobility cup group, compared with 3 of 114 patients (2.6%) in the unipolar cup group (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.249).

table.formatted: This did not meet the pre-specified O'Brien-Fleming stopping boundary of p < 0.0054.
table.expanded: This did not meet the pre-specified O'Brien-Fleming stopping boundary of p < 0.0054.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < 0.0054", Text = "This did not meet the pre-specified O'Brien-Fleming stopping boundary of p < 0.0054."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.title: Non-Significant P Value Check
stat_p_nonsig.summary_text: We found 1 non-significant p value that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

table.expanded: Decision: At the interim analysis, 0 dislocations occurred in 101 patients (0%) in the dual mobility cup group, compared with 3 of 114 patients (2.6%) in the unipolar cup group (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.249).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.249", Sentence = "Decision: At the interim analysis, 0 dislocations occurred in 101 patients (0%) in the dual mobility cup group, compared with 3 of 114 patients (2.6%) in the unipolar cup group (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.249)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::
